segments.text: Today we're looking at how CPU caches work and why they matter for performance.
Main memory is slow compared to the processor, around a hundred nanoseconds per access.
So CPUs keep small, fast copies of recently used data close to the cores.
There are usually three levels: L1, L2 and L3, each bigger and slower.
Data moves in cache lines of 64 bytes, not single bytes.
That means reading one value pulls its neighbours in for free.
This is why iterating an array in order is much faster than chasing pointers.
Linked lists scatter nodes across memory, so every step can be a cache miss.
When two cores write to the same cache line you get false sharing.
Padding hot fields onto separate lines can fix that.
Prefetchers guess what you'll read next, but only for simple patterns.
To sum up, keep hot data small, contiguous, and owned by one core.
